options: A file format for exporting reports
A collection of functions, operators, and constants combined into formulas to calculate values
A Power Query transformation step
A type of chart in Power BI
questions.explain: DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language used to create new information from data already in your Power BI model.

questions.q: What happens when you drag a numeric column onto a card visual without writing any DAX?
options: Power BI shows an error requiring a measure first
Power BI automatically summarizes it (e.g., sums it) with no formula needed
Nothing is displayed until a DAX formula is written
The column is automatically converted to a calculated column
questions.explain: Power BI can sum, count, or average a dragged field automatically — DAX becomes necessary only when you need something more specific.

questions.q: Which kind of question typically requires a DAX formula rather than automatic summarization?
options: Displaying a column's values in a table
Showing the total of a single column
Renaming a field in the Data pane
Comparing this quarter's sales to the previous quarter's
questions.explain: Comparisons across time periods require filtering to a specific subset of rows — something automatic summarization alone can't do.

questions.q: In the formula 'Total Sales = SUM(Sales[SalesAmount])', what's the benefit of creating this as a named measure instead of just dragging the field?
options: It automatically creates a matching calculated column
It calculates faster than a dragged field in every case
There is no benefit — they're functionally identical in every use
The named measure can be referenced inside other, more complex formulas
questions.explain: Once a measure like Total Sales exists, you can reuse it as a building block inside other DAX formulas instead of repeating the same aggregation.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which function is described as the single most important function in DAX?
options: CALCULATE
FILTER
SUM
IF
questions.explain: CALCULATE modifies filter context and underlies most advanced DAX formulas — important enough that this chapter gives it two dedicated lessons.
